messages.subject: distance traveled
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christen
I wonder if there is any way to calculate the daily distance traveled in the ctmm package?
My data is every 10 minutes only if the dog is moving, but I have found some data where the GPS recorded positions only during the morning, for example, and it is unlikely that the dog is not moving for 12 hours, so I attribute it to some GPS error. And I don't know how to use this data to calculate the daily distance traveled, because the number of locations is not standard for all my individuals.
What would you suggest in this case? Any bibliographic reference would also help.

Thank you,
Best

Lorena

messages.subject: Re: distance traveled
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lorena,

The manuscript on this material method was just accepted, so I won't have a reference for a couple of weeks.

The speed() function outputs the mean speed, which you can just multiply by the period of time, such as range(DATA$t), to get distance traveled.

Telemetry error can be accounted for in speed(), the same as most all other ctmm functionality, following vignette('error').

Irregular sampling and different sampling schedules is also not a problem, because everything is done in continuous time.

The real complication with speed/distance estimation, at present, is with changes in behavioral states. If your dogs are active during one period of the day, and inactive during another period of the day, then you will want to break up the data for an active movement model and an inactive movement model. In the future, we will have models that can do this in the package, but for now you have to reasonably segment the data yourself.

GPS data that are conditionally collected based on accelerometer data can add another complication, in that the missingness of the data implies a lack of movement. However, if running any analysis that doesn't know about this property (which is every out-of-the-box method that can handle gaps), the animal will be assumed to be moving in the gaps just as much as when the GPS data are being collected. In the future, we will be able to use recovered accelerometer data to bridge these gaps, but for the moment you extra need to be careful when working with these kinds of data (in any movement analysis).

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Estimating COV and COV.mu
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'd like to try to use COV and COV.mu as a way to measure model fit, so I'd like to tell ctmm to estimate these values. However, I'm not sure how to request these values. I've tried the following commands but upon inspection of the resulting ctmm object I don't see COV or COV.mu slots. Can you let me know what I'm doing wrong?

ctmm.select(tel, CTMM=GUESS, method="pHREML", control=list(method="pNewton"), COV=TRUE)

ctmm.fit(tel, CTMM=GUESS, method="pHREML", control=list(method="pNewton"), COV=TRUE)

ctmm.select(tel, CTMM=GUESS, method="pHREML", control=list(method="pNewton"), verbose=TRUE)

Thank you!

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Estimating COV and COV.mu
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

If you do

FIT <- ctmm.select(tel, CTMM=GUESS)

then the FIT object should have slots COV and COV.mu, which you can access via

FIT$COV

and

FIT$COV.mu

You should be able to see the names of the slots of the FIT object with names(FIT). On the other hand, the str() function does not like custom object classes and will not show you their slot names, if that is what you tried. I need to write a custom str.ctmm() method for that to work correctly. Similarly with printing the object out on the command line.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Convergence in path simulations etc.
messages.body_plain:
Hey Chris,

thank you very much for your quick response and help. Unfortunately, a problem with my simulation script occurred while realizing the convergence criterium (see point 1 of your answer)

I have calculated the ratio of the error using the approach you suggested from the speed function. That worked very well. However, since my a priori defined relative error has not been achieved with the number of simulations I have done so far, I came back to my simulations script.

Although I did not change anything in the script since the last time I have used it, I now run in the following error when trying to simulate a movement track based on my foraging bouts.

Here is the part of my script that leads to the error:

CSIMS <- lapply(1:n, function(r){ctmm::simulate(TeleObject,
+                                                       CTMM = FIT_sub[[paste0('Bout_',i)]],
+                                                       dt = 0.25 %#% 'min')})
Error in if (DT[i] <= dt.max) { : argument is of length zero

As a reminder, I created a subset of foraging bouts for my individuals, mean centered those bouts, fitted a movement model using the mean centered data and detrended the data later on by adding the mean of each foraging bout to the model mu to get a single model per foraging bout.

Using the point locations of a foraging bout and the respective model, I simulated n = 50 movement tracks with a temporal resolution of 15 seconds using the code snipped provided above. However, that does not work anymore. I tried doing everything again using my old code but it does not work anymore (see error message above).

I am out of ideas at that point. Do you have any idea what could cause that (ctmm version etc.) respectively how to fix it? I am using ctmm version 0.5.6.

Thank you very much in advance.

All the best,

Ines

>
> Hey Chris,
>
>

>
>
> After finishing that part I am currently working on the quantification of uncertainties. During the first part I have simulated 100 paths per foraging bout to calculate the time spent in a particular area. I took the median per simulations set. However, my question is if there is a way to find out after how many simulations convergence is reached and how I can test that? Furthermore, I don’t know if it is of relevance, but the considered foraging bouts had varying durations, meaning that the simulations were based on different numbers of recorded locations. Do you think that might have an influence on the convergence?
>
>
> Furthermore, a more general question popped up while working on the uncertainty quantification. I am planning to use Monte Carlo sampling to randomly select one movement path from each simulation set and one environmental parameter (also a simulation set) and iteratively calculate my analysis result again. By this I hope to gain an overview of the range of uncertainty. However, during literature review I found the Latin Hypercube method which is said to sample more reliable (https://lumina.com/latin-hypercube-vs-monte-carlo-sampling/). Do you have any idea when it is appropriate to use which of the two methods? I guess with an appropriate number of movement simulations I should get a good idea of the probability distributions. For my environmental parameters I already managed to derive probability distributions which are reasonable. So, in case I would use Monte Carlo, given that I use enough iterations, this should provide me with reasonable results, right? So I don’t really get when Latin Hypercube is better, when I don’t know the underlying probability distributions? Or when I use only small number of iterations? Sorry, I know this is only indirectly related to ctmm but I thought, as a statistician you might have an idea about this topic.
>
>
> Finally, I have a question regarding the choice of ctmm to reconstruct the movement paths for my analysis. One comment of a reviewer of my paper addressed exactly that: “Doing the analysis on the reconstructed trajectories rather than on the raw data is not a simple or intuitive choice so please explain this decision a bit more”. I know, that this method is more reliable and on top, allows for uncertainty assessment. However, I was so far not able to find an explanation in one of your publications. The only explanation I included was the following one, but that was obviously not enough :(.
>
> ·
>
> When considering an animals’ activities and behaviors, many quantities must be conditioned upon that individual’s movement trajectory. These quantities include, but are not limited to, distance traveled, speed, regions occupied, environmental covariates utilized, behavioral states and energy expended. (C. H. Fleming et al., 2016)  <-- Do you explain that anywhere else in more detail?
>
> Many, many questions from my side again. Thank you very much in advance for your time and help.
>
>
> All the best,
>
> Ines

messages.subject: Re: Extract the grid from a large UD object
messages.subject_clean: Extract the grid from a large UD object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Teague,

I'm not familiar with adehabitatHR formats, but for the UD object the grid information is in UD$r, where UD$r$x are the x-coordinates of the rows and UD$r$y are the y-coordinates of the columns.

Yes, the projection should stay fixed during analysis. You can also check it with the projection() method.

There is no UD re-projection method yet in ctmm, though eventually there will be for plotting on maps. However, I think if you export to a raster, then you can re-project that.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Combining multiple home ranges into an "annual home range", then computing overlap across >2 years
messages.subject_clean: Combining multiple home ranges into an "annual home range", then computing overlap across >2 years
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris and others,

I'm working with telemetry data collected from individual birds which seem to have multiple home ranges within a breeding season. I gather from the course in Feb 2019 and also from posts to this group that it's not (currently) possible to use ctmm to model multiple home ranges all at once, so I've created separate datasets and modeled these as separate HRs (each with a stable variogram), e.g. HR 1a, 1b, 1c etc.

For some of these individuals I have data from multiple years, and for those individuals I'd like to compute overlap of the "combined annual HR" across years.

I have two questions:

1. Can I combine more than one HR from a single individual into an "annual HR"?

2. Once I've done that, can i compute overlap across more than two years? (this question applies even if I can't combine HRs, i.e. can we compute overlap of HRs from >2 years)

If neither of those is currently possible using standard ctmm functions, do you know any ctmm tricks or other packages that I could use to make it work?

Many thanks for your help,

Mark

messages.subject: extract individual UD raster values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I have created multiple CTMM object of individuals, per season. I have supervised landcover class rasters each of the season.

I created UD polygons of the OUF objects using the following code:

poly.JC9.hd2 <- SpatialPolygonsDataFrame.UD(JC9.hd2.AKDES$OUF)
projection(poly.JC9.hd2)
writeOGR(obj=poly.JC9.hd2, dsn="D:/MY DRIVE/ATREE/PhD/Manuscripts/Home Range", layer="JC9hd2",
         driver="ESRI Shapefile")

 (JC9 is my individual, hd2 is the season).

Thereafter, I used the ML polygon to cut the classified raster, so that I have a classified image, indicating different landcover classes, available to this particular individual. I need to weight the available land cover classes based on the utilisation distribution of the individual.

I can obtain the UD values through the following code:

JC9.UD<- JC9.hd2.AKDES$OUF$PDF

However, this UD gives me the PDF values for ~237 points. My dataframe for this individual has 3362 locations -- and I have corresponding landcover values for these 3362  locations -- indicating the landcover class at each location.

Could you suggest how do I now assign UD as weight to the landcover classes, since the dataframe lengths do not match - 237 UD values vs 3362 points.

Also, is there a way to extract the UD values, with the corresponding coordinates, as a dataframe. I used the following code which did not quite work:

JC9.UD.coord<- as.data.frame(JC9.hd2.AKDES$OUF$r$x, JC9.hd2.AKDES$OUF$r$y, JC9.hd2.AKDES$OUF$PDF)

Can I also export this UD as a raster layer?

I can share the datafile is required.

Thanks in advance!

Regards,
Anjan Katna
ATREE
AniMove 2017

messages.subject: Re: Combining multiple home ranges into an "annual home range", then computing overlap across >2 years
messages.subject_clean: Combining multiple home ranges into an "annual home range", then computing overlap across >2 years
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

1. You can presently combine multiple UDs into a joint UD via the mean() function. Its not done in a statistically optimal way, but its not terrible.
2. In (1.) the uncertainties are not currently propagated correctly, and so I don't think the overlap code will work correctly on the averaged densities. How soon do you need this feature by?

Best,
Chris

On Thursday, October 17, 2019 at 6:44:50 PM UTC-4, Mark Bidwell wrote:

>
> For some of these individuals I have data from multiple years, and for those individuals I'd like to compute overlap of the "combined annual HR" across years.

>
> Many thanks for your help,
>
> Mark

messages.subject: Re: extract individual UD raster values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Anjan,

UD$PDF is an array where the rows have x-coordinates UD$r$x and the columns have y-coordinates UD$r$y. Storing this as a data frame would triple the memory cost.

In your export code you have DF="CDF", which exports the cumulative distribution function. These quantiles are 0% at the mode and 100% at infinity.  Other options to export are the PDF and PMF, which are 0 at infinity and positive in higher-density regions.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Detecting x-axes units of plot.variogram
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm producing plots of ctmm variograms as part of an automated process for many animals. In one variogram plot, I draw a vertical line at which a 95% decay in position autocorrelation occurs.

plot.variogram has a helpful features that automatically adjusts units for you. E.g. if the xlim is small enough it will be in hours, if larger it will be in days. This is really nice but in order to draw a vertical line, I need to know the units. If I assume hours, then when the plot converts to days the vertical line is placed in the wrong location.

Here is an example of my code:

#mod is a ctmm model
#vg is an empirical variogram

p95h <- mod$tau['position'] * -log(0.05)/3600 #hours
plot(vg,CTMM=mod, xlim=c(0,p95h*1.5 %#% 'hour'))

 #will plot correctly when plot units are in hours, but not otherwise.
abline(v=p95h,lty='dashed')

title('95% decay in position autocorrelation')

One approach would be to use units=FALSE, and always work in seconds, but this makes the plots hard to interpret. Instead, is there a way to determine what the units of the plot will be, so that I can adjust the units accordingly?

Thank you!

Ben

messages.subject: Re: extract individual UD raster values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Anjan,

Good question. akde() does not re-normalize the density estimate. Instead, there is an error argument (error=0.001 by default) that targets error in probability mass to be less than error, where most of that error is from truncation of the kernels---the integration of probability mass within cells should be much more accurate. If you used the default error=0.001 argument, then a total probability mass above 0.999 is consistent with that target.

https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/akde.html

Best,
Chris

I have added the some code into the variogram plots, which you can find in the GitHub development version:

The necessary variables are stored in the plot.env environment, which you can list via

ls(ctmm:::plot.env)

and the variable you want is

get("x.scale",envir=ctmm:::plot.env)

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I am crunching home ranges using ctmm for goitered gazelle in Mongolia.  I have the data parsed by year, season, year-season, etc.  When I run the home ranges, sometimes I get OU anistrophic as the best model, sometimes OUF anistrophic, sometimes IID.  Does it matter if you are using different models to calculate home ranges or do you need to stay with one model.  OUF anistrophic is usually the second choice when OU anistrophic is first.

Also, sometimes the 'guess' parameter does not show up when I execute the code.  I close R and re-open, but that does not fix it.  Any ideas?

Thanks, Nanette.

messages.subject: Re: choosing a model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nanette,

You always want to condition AKDE on the best model. The best model can be different if either the movement is different or the sampling is different. If its the latter case, then that isn't a statement about what the animal is or isn't doing, but what you can or can't resolve from the data.

With ctmm.guess, be careful to either do this

GUESS <- ctmm.guess(DATA,interactive=FALSE)

or this

ctmm.guess(DATA) # click 'save' when finished

but not this

GUESS <- ctmm.guess(DATA)

Best,
Chris
